counterfactuals.output:
**Thai Court Finds Former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra Guilty in Landmark Land-Deal Case**

**Bangkok** — Thailand’s Supreme Court has found former Prime Minister **Thaksin Shinawatra** guilty of abusing his authority in connection with a controversial Bangkok land purchase by his then-wife, marking one of the most significant legal rulings in the long-running political conflict that has divided Thailand for years.

The verdict centers on a **2003 land deal** involving a prime plot in Bangkok’s **Ratchadaphisek area**, purchased by Thaksin’s then-wife, **Pojaman Shinawatra**, from a state-linked financial institution. The court ruled that Thaksin, who was prime minister at the time, violated conflict-of-interest laws by allowing the transaction to proceed while he held ultimate political authority over state agencies connected to the sale.

Thaksin denied wrongdoing, describing the case as politically motivated and part of a broader campaign by his opponents to dismantle his influence. He was not present in court for the ruling, having left Thailand earlier and entered self-imposed exile.

## The Ratchadaphisek Land Deal

The case focused on land sold by the **Financial Institutions Development Fund**, a unit linked to the Bank of Thailand that had taken over assets from failed financial firms after the 1997 Asian financial crisis.

In 2003, Pojaman successfully bid for the land at a price prosecutors said was favorable. Although she was the buyer, prosecutors argued that Thaksin’s position as prime minister created a prohibited conflict of interest because government bodies under his administration had influence over the state-linked seller.

The court concluded that Thaksin breached laws designed to prevent public officials from having an interest in contracts involving state agencies. Pojaman was acquitted in the same case, with the court finding that the legal restriction applied specifically to Thaksin as a public officeholder.

The ruling carried major symbolic weight because it was among the first major corruption-related judgments against Thaksin after his removal from power.

## Thaksin’s Rise and Removal

Thaksin, a telecommunications billionaire, founded the **Thai Rak Thai Party** and swept to power in 2001. His government became hugely popular among rural and working-class voters through policies such as low-cost health care, village development funds, and debt relief programs.

But his critics accused him of corruption, authoritarianism, conflicts of interest, and using state power to benefit his family’s business interests. Tensions intensified after the 2006 sale of his family’s telecom conglomerate, **Shin Corp**, to Singapore’s Temasek Holdings in a tax-free transaction that triggered public outrage among opponents.

In September 2006, while Thaksin was abroad, the military staged a coup and removed him from office. The coup leaders accused his government of corruption, abuse of power, and undermining democratic institutions. Thaksin rejected the allegations and said the coup was an attack on democracy.

After the coup, his Thai Rak Thai Party was dissolved, but parties aligned with him continued to win elections, reflecting his deep support base in the countryside, especially in Thailand’s north and northeast.

## Exile and Legal Battles

Thaksin returned to Thailand briefly in 2008 to face legal proceedings after a pro-Thaksin party won elections and formed a government. However, as court cases and political pressure mounted, he left the country again, saying he would not receive a fair trial under a system influenced by his political enemies.

He spent years in exile, moving between countries including the United Kingdom, the United Arab Emirates, and others, while continuing to exert influence over Thai politics from abroad. Thai authorities sought his return to serve prison sentences in cases linked to corruption and abuse of power.

For supporters, Thaksin remained a symbol of electoral democracy and policies that improved rural livelihoods. For opponents, he represented corruption, populism, and the capture of state institutions for personal and family gain.

## Political Protests and National Division

The verdict came against a backdrop of intense political unrest in Thailand.

The country had been deeply polarized between pro- and anti-Thaksin forces. The anti-Thaksin **People’s Alliance for Democracy**, known as the **Yellow Shirts**, led street protests accusing governments aligned with Thaksin of acting as his proxies. They argued that electoral victories by pro-Thaksin parties did not erase corruption allegations and that Thaksin’s influence had to be removed from Thai politics.

On the other side, Thaksin’s supporters—many of whom later organized under the **Red Shirt** movement—said the courts, military, and conservative establishment were working together to overturn the will of the electorate. They viewed legal cases against Thaksin and his allies as politically selective.

Protests escalated throughout 2008. Demonstrators occupied government buildings and demanded the resignation of governments linked to Thaksin. Thailand’s politics became increasingly unstable, with court rulings, mass demonstrations, and military pressure shaping the political landscape as much as elections.

The unrest reflected a deeper struggle over power in Thailand: between elected governments backed by rural majorities and an establishment network including royalist conservatives, parts of the bureaucracy, the military, and urban middle-class activists.

## Broader Significance

The court’s decision against Thaksin was more than a corruption verdict; it became a defining moment in Thailand’s political crisis. It reinforced the legal campaign against him while deepening the sense among his supporters that the justice system was being used as a political weapon.

For his opponents, the ruling validated years of accusations that Thaksin abused power while in office. For his supporters, it confirmed their belief that unelected institutions were determined to neutralize a leader who repeatedly won popular mandates through elections.

The verdict did not end Thaksin’s role in Thai politics. Instead, it became another chapter in a prolonged conflict that continued to shape Thailand for years, contributing to further protests, court interventions, military involvement, and repeated cycles of political instability.

BANGKOK — Thailand’s Supreme Court found ousted former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra guilty of corruption Tuesday and sentenced him in absentia to two years in prison, deepening a political crisis that has already brought months of street protests and left the elected government struggling to assert control.

Thaksin, removed by the military in a 2006 coup, fled to Britain earlier this year rather than face trial, saying he could not expect justice from courts he says have been influenced by his political enemies. The verdict marks the first criminal conviction against the billionaire telecoms tycoon, whose rise to power transformed Thai politics and whose influence continues to divide the country.

The court ruled that Thaksin abused his authority while in office by helping his then-wife, Pojaman, purchase a prime Bangkok land plot from a state agency in 2003. Judges said the transaction violated laws barring government officials and their spouses from doing business with state bodies under their supervision.

Thaksin has denied wrongdoing. His supporters say the case is part of a broader campaign by the military, judiciary and royalist establishment to dismantle his political movement. His opponents say the conviction proves he used public office for personal gain.

The ruling comes as Bangkok remains gripped by protests led by the People’s Alliance for Democracy, a royalist, nationalist movement that has occupied the grounds of Government House since August and is demanding the resignation of the pro-Thaksin government.

The PAD accuses the current administration of serving as a proxy for Thaksin, whose allies returned to power in elections last year after the military-backed government lifted a ban on politics. Protest leaders say Thailand’s electoral system has been corrupted by vote-buying and populist policies that made Thaksin overwhelmingly popular among rural and working-class voters.

The government says it was democratically elected and has accused the protesters of trying to overturn the will of the electorate. Clashes between pro- and anti-government groups have raised fears of wider unrest in a country still recovering from the 2006 coup.

Thaksin, who built his political base with low-cost health care, village development funds and debt relief programs, remains deeply popular in the north and northeast. But he is reviled by many in Bangkok’s middle class and among conservative elites, who accuse him of authoritarianism, corruption and disloyalty to national institutions.

His flight to the United Kingdom has further complicated Thailand’s political standoff. Authorities are expected to seek his extradition, though legal proceedings could take months or longer. Thaksin has substantial business and personal ties abroad and has previously said he intends to continue defending himself from outside the country.

The conviction also places renewed pressure on Prime Minister Somchai Wongsawat, Thaksin’s brother-in-law, who took office after a court removed his predecessor, Samak Sundaravej, for violating conflict-of-interest rules. The PAD has rejected Somchai’s leadership and vowed to continue its protests until the government steps down.

Thailand has seen repeated cycles of elections, court rulings, protests and military intervention since Thaksin’s ouster. Tuesday’s verdict is unlikely to end the struggle over his legacy — and may instead harden the divisions between those who see him as a champion of the poor and those who regard him as a threat to Thailand’s political order.
